summary: Defines functional requirements for the directory services of domain registries, plus common base requirements for extending these to other Internet registries. Registries expose data via varying directory services, and this document sets goals for a common approach. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Different registries keep lists of who owns what, each using their own way to look things up. This lists the things a shared lookup system should be able to do.

subtitle: What a unified protocol for querying domain registries should be able to do.

tldr.problem: Domain registries and registrars expose their data via different directory services with incompatible formats, and extensions like whois, rwhois, LDAP, and XML each have different quirks, security, and capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: CRISP (Cross Registry Internet Service Protocol) requirements specify a unified set of functional and feature capabilities that any directory service protocol must support to work across multiple registries.
tldr.outcome: The requirements enable future protocols to support lookups and searches across registries while accommodating privacy policies, access controls, IPv6 addresses, and internationalized domain names in a standard way.

today: RFC 3707 is an Informational document that set the functional baseline for what CRISP (Cross Registry Internet Service Protocol) protocols should support. It remains the requirements specification for unified registry directory services. While the CRISP protocol itself did not see widespread adoption, the requirements continue to inform how registry directory services are designed.

sections.title: The Registry Lookup Problem
sections.content:
As the Internet grew, the centralized Network Information Center (NIC) became many autonomous, distributed registries. Each exposed its data through different directory services: the whois protocol (RFC 954), rwhois (RFC 2167), LDAP, or custom formats.

These services vary widely in syntax, capabilities, security mechanisms, and what data they return. RFC 3707 sets common functional requirements so a new unified protocol could eventually replace them all while serving multiple registry types: domain registries, Regional Internet Registries (RIRs), routing registries, and incident contact registries.
sections.plainLanguage: There are many different databases of who owns what on the Internet. Each one uses its own weird language to look things up. This document lists the things any new shared language should be able to do.

sections.title: Registry Types and Communities
sections.content:
Domain registries (thick or thin) maintain TLD delegations and domain registrant contact data. Registrars accept registrations on behalf of registries. Regional Internet Registries (RIRs) allocate IP address space and autonomous system numbers by geographic region. Routing registries (IRRs) store routing policy using RPSL. Incident contact registries let network operators register emergency contacts.

The protocol must also serve diverse end users: registrants, service providers, trademark holders, law enforcement, certificate authorities, and DNS users seeking to troubleshoot problems. Some may be abusive, trying to harvest data for spam or attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Many different groups use registries: shops that sell names, people that manage IP numbers, people that list routing rules, and people investigating problems. The protocol has to work for all of them.

sections.title: Base Functional Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol MUST support mining prevention by allowing servers to rate-limit queries. It MUST use existing technology standards, not reinvent solutions at every layer. Schemas MUST be standard and extensible, defined in a common schema language that supports future data types. The protocol MUST allow granular access control: anonymous access, authenticated access, and role-based permissions, with a mechanism for clients to query what access they have.

Responses must be machine-parsable. Entities must be uniquely referenceable across servers. The protocol must NOT require data aggregation to a central repository (decentralization is required). Authentication must be optional and flexible. Base error responses MUST distinguish permission denied, not found, and insufficient resources. Servers must support protocol and schema versioning negotiation. Privacy labels must mark data with do not redistribute or special access granted.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared system should let servers slow down information thieves, work with common tools, use the same schemas, let people request only what they are allowed to see, be safe to automate, and work when things change.

sections.title: Domain-Specific Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol MUST support three lookups: contact lookup by unique reference, nameserver lookup by hostname or IP, and domain lookup by fully-qualified name. It MUST support three searches: domain name search (exact or partial, with internationalization support), domain registrant search by name, and domains hosted on a nameserver.

Data schemas MUST express domain activation status, registrant, nameservers, contact roles, delegating registry, and registrar. Schemas must support arbitrary extensions and off-line serialization for backup and recovery. Servers must be able to truncate large result sets and explain why (performance or policy). Result limits must distinguish empty results, performance-driven truncation, and privacy-driven truncation. The protocol must use DNS delegation authority to find authoritative servers and support both thick and thin registry models in a distributed fashion.
sections.plainLanguage: You should be able to look up a domain, find who owns it, find what servers handle it, search for domains by owner, and understand when a list is cut short.

sections.title: Feature and Security Requirements
sections.content:
The protocol MUST support client authentication with room for many authentication types and future extensions. It MUST provide referrals and entity references with a common referral scheme. A relay bag mechanism allows referring servers to pass opaque coordination data (for auditing or tracking) to referring clients, which pass it onward to the referent server.

The protocol MUST support structured queries and responses using a pre-existing schema language with defined schemas. Data omission must be expressible in three ways: complete omission, permission denied, or privacy constraint. The protocol must support internationalization: UTF-8 text with language tags, and multiple character sets in contact data. Future protocols must protect against denial-of-service attacks and unauthorized data mining when supporting distributed query meshes.
sections.plainLanguage: Clients should be able to prove who they are, get redirected to the right server, ask questions a computer can parse, and understand why data is hidden.
